name: Old Babylonian Empire (Hammurabi)

areaKm2.note: Seshat codes Polity Territory 400,000-500,000 km2 for Amorite Babylonia (2000-1600 BCE), Taagepera 1978 gives 0.25 million km2 at 1690 BCE (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_largest_empires). The historical-basemaps world_bc2000 polygon 'Ur' (nearest file before 1750; covers Babylon, Sippar, Larsa, Eshnunna and Assur) measures ~341,000 km2 computed from the GeoJSON. Mari and the middle Euphrates are outside that polygon.

population.note: OWID historical population (https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/population.csv?v=1&csvType=full&useColumnShortNames=true): Iraq 0.875 M in 2000 BCE and 1.25 M in 1000 BCE, linear to 1750 BCE = 0.97 M, covering nearly all of Hammurabi's realm (Mari on the middle Euphrates adds little). Seshat codes Amorite Babylonia's population as not available (https://seshat-db.com/core/polity/479).

urbanization.note: Educated guess. Southern Mesopotamia remained densely urban; Seshat codes the largest Isin-Larsa period settlement at 175,000-225,000, which looks high.

activePersonnel.note: Hamblin 2006, Warfare in the Ancient Near East to 1600 BC, ch. 7 (Mari archive): Shamshi-Adad wrote that 6,000 men from Mari, 10,000 from Assyria and 6,000 from allied Eshnunna would make 'a strong army' of 20,000, implying most armies of the age were smaller; a Mari report puts an enemy force at 15,000; Hammurabi himself warned that 1,000 troops sent are rumoured as 10,000. After 1763-1761 Hammurabi held Larsa, Eshnunna and Mari, so he could field roughly what three kingdoms combined could. Low = one strong field army; high = field army plus garrisons in conquered Mari, Eshnunna and Larsa. audit 2026-10-30: grade C -> D: cited by ISBN only, with no fetched copy of the book (SOURCES.md grading rule).

trainedReserves.note: Educated guess. Ilkum field holders callable within a month.

supportPersonnel.note: Educated guess. Boat crews, scribes, quartermasters, the few chariot crews.

mobilizationRatio.note: Educated guess. The ilkum system granted fields for military service, making a large share of free men liable; Old Babylonian armies drew heavily on these holders.

mobilizable.note: population x mobilizationRatio (low x low, mid x mid, high x high).

count.note: Hamblin 2006, Warfare in the Ancient Near East to 1600 BC, ch. 7 (Mari archive): Shamshi-Adad wrote that 6,000 men from Mari, 10,000 from Assyria and 6,000 from allied Eshnunna would make 'a strong army' of 20,000, implying most armies of the age were smaller; a Mari report puts an enemy force at 15,000; Hammurabi himself warned that 1,000 troops sent are rumoured as 10,000. After 1763-1761 Hammurabi held Larsa, Eshnunna and Mari, so he could field roughly what three kingdoms combined could. Split: close-order spear and axe infantry (redum soldiers) ~55%. audit 2026-10-30: grade C -> D: cited by ISBN only, with no fetched copy of the book (SOURCES.md grading rule).

training.note: Mostly ilkum holders and levies (rubric 0.25-0.5), some professional troops.

Educated guess. Horse-drawn chariots existed in the Mari period but were rare and largely royal; chariot armies only spread after ~1600 BCE. Crews are in supportPersonnel.

quality.note: Early, heavier chariots, a generation before the Late Bronze Age light chariot.

training.note: Elite crews but no chariot tactics yet.

commandQuality.note: Rubric 0.5-0.75: Hammurabi was a proven strategist (sequenced wars against Larsa, Eshnunna, Mari; flooding tactics); generalship good, no staff system.

cohesion.note: Rubric 0.25-0.5: coalition warfare of shifting Amorite kingdoms; core Babylonian troops more cohesive.

weapons.note: Between anchor 1 and 2: tin bronze, composite bows, early chariots but no chariot armies.

armor.note: Between anchor 1 and 2: helmets, some leather and early scale armour.

ships.note: Anchor 1: river boats used for troop and grain transport.

fortification.note: Between 1 and 2: massive mudbrick walls (Babylon, Mari, Eshnunna), siege towers and rams attested in Mari texts.

logistics.note: Between 1 and 2: river transport, palace granaries, ration lists; ilkum supply system.

communications.note: Between 1 and 2: dense royal correspondence by courier (Mari letters) and fire signals.

isr.note: Year anchor ~1.4: envoys, spies and informant reports are frequent in the Mari letters.

gdpPerCapita.note: Maddison Project 2023 via https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/gdp-per-capita-maddison-project-database.csv?v=1&csvType=full&useColumnShortNames=true: Iraq 1 CE = 1,116, 730 CE = 1,466 (2011 int$). Old Babylonian contracts show a monetised silver economy with hired labour; scaled slightly below the 1 CE value.

gdp.note: population x gdpPerCapita (low x low, mid x mid, high x high).

milSpendShare.note: Educated guess. Soldiers were mostly paid in field allotments (ilkum), not cash.

industrialShare.note: Educated guess. Craft and trade economy (textiles, metal, long-distance trade).

foodSurplus.note: Educated guess. Irrigated agriculture; recurrent salinisation in the south.

annualCohort.note: population x 0.0095: Hansen 2006 (https://ancientportsantiques.com/wp-content/uploads/Documents/PLACES/GreeceContinental/Athens-Hansen2006.pdf, p. 34) puts a year class of 18-19-year-olds at ca. 1.9% of all males in a pre-modern age structure, i.e. ~0.95% of total population reaching military age per year (males only). Same model as the classical snapshots; Bronze Age life expectancy was if anything lower, so this is not an underestimate.

roadKm.note: Educated guess. No engineered roads; river, canal and caravan routes.

majorPorts.note: Educated guess. River ports at Sippar, Babylon, Ur, Mari.

merchantTonnage.note: Educated guess. River boats of a few tons and Gulf trade via Dilmun.

supplyRangeKm.note: Educated guess. Armies followed the rivers with boat supply; Mari letters show armies short of grain away from them.

draftAnimals.note: Educated guess. ~0.1-0.13 donkeys and oxen per inhabitant.

chokepoints: Diyala route to Elam and the Zagros

homeDefense.note: Rubric 1.1-1.2: familiar alluvium, walled cities and canals that could be used for flooding.

notes: Snapshot = 1750 BCE (middle chronology), after Hammurabi's conquest of Larsa (1763), Eshnunna and Mari (1761). Chariots are listed only as a token royal arm because the horse chariot was not yet a mass weapon in Mesopotamia; the chariot-archetype doctrine fits poorly. Army numbers are reconstructed from Mari-archive letters as discussed by Hamblin (2006), not from any census. Population convention: everything inside the border.
